analysis.one_liner: Limits federal drug enforcement powers over pharmaceutical registrants while speeding new drug scheduling.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a Senate committee the day it was introduced and died there when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015, with no committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how the federal government polices companies that make and distribute controlled substances. It would let a company facing DEA license suspension or revocation submit a 'corrective action plan' that could delay or end the proceeding, and it would write a narrow legal definition of 'imminent danger to the public health or safety' — the standard DEA uses to immediately pull a distributor's license. It would also require the Attorney General to schedule newly approved drugs within 45 days of a health department recommendation, skip normal agency review steps, and decide registration applications for clinical-trial drugs within 180 days. It never got a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, wholesale drug distributors, and pharmacies whose DEA registrations are threatened: the corrective action plan process and the narrow 'imminent danger' definition make it harder for the government to quickly suspend or revoke a registration over suspected diversion. Companies seeking to run clinical trials also gain from guaranteed registration decisions within 180 days.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Attorney General to make a final decision on a clinical-trial registration application within 180 days, or give written notice of outstanding issues and an estimated decision date [S2] [S3].

Directs the Attorney General to issue an interim final rule within 45 days placing a newly recommended, never-marketed drug into the schedule HHS recommends, bypassing the findings normally required and making the rule effective immediately [S2] [S3].

Lets a registrant facing denial, revocation, or suspension submit a corrective action plan that the Attorney General must review to decide whether to discontinue or defer the proceeding, and defines 'imminent danger' narrowly (outside professional practice, foreseeable risk of death or abuse, or diversion) [S2] [S3].

Directs HHS, FDA, and CDC to report to Congress on obstacles to legitimate patient access, diversion issues, and how collaboration between law enforcement and the pharmaceutical industry can benefit patients [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, communities affected by prescription-drug diversion would bear the cost of slower enforcement: the corrective action plan process creates a window in which a distributor suspected of diversion could keep operating, and the narrow 'imminent danger' definition limits the government's tool for immediate suspensions. Patient safety gains depend largely on a study rather than on enforceable rules.

drawbacks.text: The corrective action plan option and the narrowed 'imminent danger' definition give suspected diverters procedural room to avoid or delay losing their registration, weakening the immediate suspension tool [S2] [S3].

The mandatory 45-day scheduling deadline strips out the Attorney General's independent findings requirement, leaving scheduling of a brand-new drug to a fast-tracked rule that binds immediately [S2] [S3].
The bill's public-facing substance — the report on patient access and diversion — is a study with no enforcement deadline attached, while its binding provisions all run in favor of registrants [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There are real arguments on both sides: legitimate pain patients were affected when enforcement shut down suppliers, and trial sponsors faced registration delays. But the binding provisions of the bill do not fix patient access directly — they mostly slow and soften enforcement against registrants suspected of diversion, at the peak of the opioid epidemic. The bill's costs fall on the same public its title invokes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on September 18, 2014, with Senator Sheldon Whitehouse joining as a cosponsor [S1] [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction, with no further action recorded [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2015, with the bill still sitting in committee — no markup, no floor vote, no law [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died without a vote, DEA enforcement authority against drug manufacturers and distributors was left unchanged for the moment; communities affected by diversion were spared the weakened enforcement standard, and registrants also gained nothing. A substantially similar bill was enacted two years later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo enforcement kept for two more years

for.role: Registrants subject to DEA enforcement under the Controlled Substances Act
for.what_they_did: Pushed Congress in this era for limits on DEA's immediate suspension and revocation authority over registrations, a campaign widely reported in connection with this legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Republican lead sponsor from Utah and a Democratic lead cosponsor from Rhode Island, plus two cosponsors split one each — and no recorded opposition; it simply died in committee without a vote [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and wholesale drug distributors
industries.note: The bill would soften the main enforcement tools used against their DEA registrations — a corrective action plan that can discontinue or defer revocation proceedings, and a narrow statutory definition of 'imminent danger to the public health or safety' limiting immediate suspensions. The gain comes at the expense of faster removal of registrants suspected of diverting prescription drugs.

Guaranteed 180-day decisions on registrations to handle controlled substances for clinical trials would cut a source of delay in drug development, which mostly runs alongside the public interest in new medicines.

The corrective action plan process would apply to pharmacies facing suspension or revocation, giving them a path to avoid losing their registration; legitimate dispensers facing mistakes could benefit, while diverting ones would too.
